title: Music Around the World
objective: After this level you can explain how musical traditions differ in scales, rhythms and instruments.
summary: Musical traditions differ in their scales, their ways of organizing time and their instruments, as the 1977 Voyager record shows. Ethnomusicology studies each music on its own terms.

cards.headline: In 1977, NASA sent 90 minutes of Earth's music into space.
cards.body: Both Voyager spacecraft carry a golden record into interstellar space, its music chosen by a committee chaired by Carl Sagan. Next to Bach and Chuck Berry sit a Javanese court gamelan, percussion from Senegal, a raga sung by Kesarbai Kerkar and a Japanese shakuhachi solo. Play them side by side and they don't sound like one music on different instruments. So what exactly changes from one tradition to the next?

cards.headline: Difference 1: the ladder of notes
cards.body: Remember Level 8? A scale is defined by its pattern of intervals, and a piano splits the octave into 12 equal semitones. Much of the world climbs other ladders. Five-note pentatonic scales turn up, in different forms, from sub-Saharan Africa to East Asia. Arabic and Indian classical music go further, using intervals smaller than a semitone. So a piano can't play every tradition's notes: some fall between its keys.

cards.headline: Differences 2 and 3: the clock and the sound
cards.body: Time is organized differently too. Indian classical music runs on a tala, a cycle of a fixed number of beats that repeats through a whole performance; Britannica notes it has no exact Western equivalent. Much African music layers contrasting rhythms at once (polyrhythm), often over a timeline pattern played on a bell. And the sound sources differ: a gamelan, the orchestra of Java and Bali, is mostly gongs and tuned metal instruments struck with mallets.

cards.headline: Hear each music on its own terms
cards.body: Level 1's definition said music follows a culture's own standards. A whole field takes that seriously: ethnomusicology, the study of all the world's musics, named around 1950 by the Dutch scholar Jaap Kunst and American colleagues. It depends on fieldwork: studying music where people make and perform it. Folkways Records, founded by Moses Asch in 1948 to document 'people's music' worldwide, has belonged to the Smithsonian since 1987. A raga isn't a major scale with wrong notes. It's a raga with the right ones.

mascot.line: Keep this for the whole chapter: hear each tradition by its own rules.

cards.headline: World music: mapped
learned: The 1977 Voyager record carries music from many traditions
Traditions differ in scales, time cycles and instruments
Ethnomusicology studies each music in its own context
Smithsonian Folkways has documented people's music since 1948

questions.prompt: Which of these is on the music selection of the 1977 Voyager Golden Record?

options.label: A recording of a rocket launch
options.rationale: The record's music ranges from Bach to Chuck Berry; launch noise isn't among the pieces.

options.label: Only European symphonies
options.rationale: It also carries music from Java, Senegal, India, Japan and more.

options.label: A single national anthem
options.rationale: The committee chose a varied 90-minute selection.

questions.explanation: The music includes a Javanese court gamelan, Senegalese percussion, Kesarbai Kerkar's raga and a shakuhachi solo, alongside Bach and Chuck Berry.

questions.prompt: An ethnomusicologist meets a raga for the first time. Which approach fits the field?

options.label: Judge it by the rules of the Western major scale
options.rationale: That measures one tradition with another's ruler.

options.label: Study it in its own context, including how it's performed
Rank it against Bach to see which is better
options.rationale: Ethnomusicology compares systems; it doesn't crown winners.

options.label: Rely only on printed scores
options.rationale: The field depends on fieldwork and live performance.

questions.explanation: Ethnomusicology studies all the world's musics on their own terms, and it depends on field research into performance.

questions.prompt: Levels 8 and 51 both note a limit of the piano. Why can't it play every note used across the world's traditions?

options.label: Its keys don't reach high or low enough for them
options.rationale: Range isn't the problem; the gaps between keys are.

options.label: Other traditions never repeat notes at the octave
options.rationale: The octave is a constant in most cultures' scales.

options.label: Pentatonic scales need more than 12 keys per octave
Some traditions use intervals smaller than a semitone

questions.explanation: Equal temperament gives 12 semitones per octave. Arabic and Indian classical music use intervals smaller than a semitone, which fall between the keys.
